impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's Penumbra framework—which holds that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis does not apply to prior art determinations under AIA § 102(d)(2)—is correct, and whether a reference patent's provisional application filing date can be used as prior art without satisfying the written description requirement for at least one claim of the non-provisional patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination and remanded, finding that the Board improperly relied on its Penumbra precedent to assign a prior art reference an earlier provisional filing date under AIA § 102(d)(2) without conducting a proper written description analysis under Dynamic Drinkware. This ruling is significant because it directly impacts how provisional application dates are used to establish prior art in IPR proceedings under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a higher threshold for challengers to establish prior art dates, as references cannot automatically claim provisional filing dates without meeting written description requirements. This makes it harder to invalidate patents using earlier-filed provisional applications.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patents in IPR proceedings face greater difficulty establishing prior art dates based on provisional applications, potentially reducing the effectiveness of inter partes review as a tool for clearing patent landscapes.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement when assessing copyright infringement damages, and what constitutes a permissible application of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine in calculating damages against the government.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's use of a hypothetical negotiation to assess copyright infringement damages for the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA® software, rather than deferring to the existing license agreement terms. However, the court vacated in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages. This case establishes important guardrails for software copyright damages methodology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's endorsement of hypothetical negotiation as a valid damages methodology, which may yield higher damages than strict adherence to license terms when infringement exceeds licensed use.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling constraining the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and prohibiting non-compensatory damages limits copyright holders' ability to recover windfall damages, and creates uncertainty about how post-infringement evidence can be used in damages calculations.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar invalidity grounds not raised in a prior IPR petition, and what evidentiary standard applies to determining whether a 'skilled searcher conducting a diligent search' reasonably could have discovered prior art references.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to support estoppel on one invalidity ground and inadequate accounting for hindsight bias on another. The court emphasized that estoppel determinations must be based on robust evidence of what a diligent search would have uncovered, not retrospective reasoning. This decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel and provides greater latitude for defendants to assert invalidity defenses in district court.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a more rigorous evidentiary standard for IPR estoppel, preserving their ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court litigation even after filing IPR petitions. This reduces the risk that filing an IPR will foreclose important prior art arguments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent owners face diminished benefits from IPR estoppel, as it becomes harder to preclude defendants from raising new invalidity theories in litigation, potentially increasing the cost and complexity of patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a jury verdict form that uses a single question covering infringement for multiple asserted patents is reversible error, and whether the district court erred in its § 101 analysis and non-infringement determinations for wireless communications patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's inclusion of a single question covering infringement for all four asserted patents was improper. The court also vacated and remanded for further § 101 analysis on one patent while affirming that two other patents were not directed to abstract ideas. This decision has significant implications for how patent trials are structured when multiple patents are asserted.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms separately address each asserted patent, providing clearer appellate review and preventing ambiguous general verdicts that could mask errors on individual patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents face increased trial complexity and the risk that consolidated verdict forms will be overturned, potentially requiring costly retrials.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' in a provisional application to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the non-provisional patent constituted an obvious typographical error correctable without adding new matter, thereby entitling the patent to the provisional's priority date and avoiding anticipation by Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's '953 patent as anticipated, holding that the change from 'C2' to 'C1' in a chemical substituent definition between the provisional and non-provisional applications was not an obvious typographical error. Because the patent could not claim priority from the provisional, Pfizer's intervening disclosure of nirmatrelvir constituted anticipating prior art. This ruling has major implications for pharmaceutical patent prosecution and provisional application drafting.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic and competing pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from strict enforcement of provisional application requirements, as errors in provisional filings can create gaps that allow intervening prior art to invalidate later patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies face heightened risk that even minor errors in provisional applications—particularly in chemical nomenclature—can be fatal to patent validity if competitors make intervening disclosures, emphasizing the need for meticulous provisional drafting.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the United States in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe class action tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that the six-year statute of limitations under 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe tolling, affirming dismissal of claims by a bank holding company and its subsidiaries that lost significant assets during the 2008 financial crisis. The court recognized that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in CalPERS v. ANZ Securities. This ruling has broad implications for financial institution claims against the government involving the 2008 financial crisis and government-sponsored enterprise investments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Financial institutions and investors who relied on class action tolling to preserve claims against the government face permanent loss of their ability to pursue breach of contract and takings claims. The elimination of American Pipe tolling for § 2501 creates a rigid filing deadline that cannot be extended by participation in related class actions.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulatory 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on timing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to express willingness to participate in sunset reviews within 15 days of the notice of initiation is a permissible exercise of Commerce's delegated authority. The statute is silent on the filing deadline, and the regulation reflects reasoned decisionmaking. This decision preserves Commerce's ability to efficiently manage antidumping sunset reviews and prevents the automatic revocation of antidumping duty orders when domestic parties miss the deadline.
impacts.positiveImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers benefit from regulatory clarity and the preservation of Commerce's procedural framework, which ensures orderly sunset review proceedings and predictable outcomes for international trade compliance.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic manufacturers risk losing antidumping protection if they fail to meet the strict 15-day participation deadline, as the regulation was upheld as valid even though the statute itself imposes no such deadline.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's payment obligation tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination, or whether the case must be transferred to a regional circuit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a contract dispute interpreting whether asserted patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination, because the dispute was fundamentally about state-law contract interpretation rather than a substantial patent law question. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This ruling clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for settlement agreement disputes that reference patent proceedings but turn on contract interpretation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies negotiating patent settlement agreements benefit from clarity that disputes over such agreements will be heard in regional circuits applying state contract law, which may provide more predictable and favorable standards than Federal Circuit patent-centric review.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent litigants may face forum uncertainty when settlement agreements contain patent-related contingencies, as the Federal Circuit's refusal to exercise jurisdiction could lead to different interpretive outcomes across regional circuits.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using relay devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional for purposes of attorney fee awards. The court found the claims were directed to collecting, analyzing, and storing farming data—an abstract concept—without inventive improvement. This ruling reinforces the application of Alice/Mayo to agricultural technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Agricultural technology companies accused of infringement benefit from strong § 101 defenses against broadly-claimed data collection patents, and the vacatur on exceptionality signals that attorney fees may be available in cases involving weak § 101 patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech startups and patent holders face continued difficulty patenting data collection and processing methods in the agricultural sector, and risk exceptional case findings and fee shifting when asserting such patents.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court abuses its discretion by awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and imposing sanctions under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 against plaintiff's counsel in a patent infringement case dismissed for failure to state a claim.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to Volkswagen under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court found the case exceptional and upheld joint and several liability for the fee award against both the plaintiff and its attorney. This case serves as a strong warning about the consequences of filing meritless patent infringement suits.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies targeted by meritless patent infringement suits benefit from robust fee-shifting and sanctions mechanisms that deter frivolous patent litigation and impose meaningful consequences on plaintiffs and their counsel.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face heightened financial risk when bringing infringement claims that are dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6), as courts may impose substantial fee awards and personal sanctions on attorneys.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury's verdict finding validity and infringement of a drug-releasing biodegradable fiber patent was supported by sufficient evidence, or whether the defendant was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on anticipation and non-infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict in favor of the University of Texas, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law on both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of a patent covering drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in coronary stents. The court found that prior art anticipated the asserted claims and that BSC's products did not meet the claim limitations. This reversal of a significant jury verdict illustrates the Federal Circuit's willingness to overturn trial outcomes on JMOL.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device companies benefit from the Federal Circuit's rigorous JMOL standard, which can overturn unfavorable jury verdicts when the evidence does not support the findings, providing a meaningful appellate safety valve in high-stakes patent disputes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and research institutions asserting patents face the risk that even successful jury verdicts may be reversed on appeal, undermining their ability to monetize patent portfolios through litigation and increasing the uncertainty of patent enforcement outcomes.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly construed the terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent claim's weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether the court permissibly waived the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta, a neurological disorder drug, based on likely infringement of Otsuka's '282 patent. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal. The ruling on claim construction—whether salt forms versus free base forms of drugs control the weight-to-weight ratio—has significant implications for Hatch-Waxman patent litigation involving combination drug products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of the preliminary injunction, which protects market exclusivity for combination drug products and provides guidance on how drug compound terms in patent claims should be interpreted.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face barriers to market entry when brand-name companies obtain preliminary injunctions, and the requirement to post bonds pending appeal imposes additional financial costs on the enjoined party.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction involving functionality determinations in design patents should be resolved by a jury.
impacts.description: The en banc Federal Circuit denied rehearing, leaving in place the panel decision applying the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement. The case generated significant division, with the Chief Judge and three other judges dissenting. The concurrence defended the current framework, while the dissent argued that Egyptian Goddess improperly shifted the infringement inquiry to focus on dissimilarities and that functionality issues in design patent claim construction should go to a jury. This denial signals continued uncertainty in design patent law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the status quo, which allows district courts to resolve design patent infringement at summary judgment based on visual dissimilarities, providing efficient case resolution without costly jury trials.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent owners face continued risk that courts will focus on differences rather than overall similarity when assessing infringement, potentially making it harder to enforce design patents. The sharp division on the court signals possible future changes to the framework.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether 'executable program code configured to' limitations in software patent claims invoke means-plus-function treatment under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) in light of the court's intervening decision in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling on the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration of whether § 112(f) means-plus-function treatment applies to 'executable program code configured to' claim terms, in light of the court's intervening Dyfan precedent. The court affirmed invalidity of a separate patent claim. This decision has significant implications for how software patent claims using 'configured to' language are construed and whether they are treated as means-plus-function limitations subject to indefiniteness challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the opportunity to argue under Dyfan that 'executable program code configured to' recites sufficient structure to avoid § 112(f), potentially saving claims from indefiniteness invalidation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending against software patent claims face uncertainty about when 'configured to' limitations invoke § 112(f), potentially extending litigation as courts reconsider claim construction under evolving precedent.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on both improper venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b) and failure to state a claim under 35 U.S.C. § 101 in the same order, or whether the venue dismissal precludes reaching the § 101 merits.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of an e-commerce patent infringement case on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds. AML argued that the court should not have reached the § 101 question after finding venue improper, but the Federal Circuit found no error in the court addressing both grounds. The '979 patent, directed to e-commerce methods using a 'bridge computer,' was held patent-ineligible. This decision confirms that courts may address § 101 eligibility even when also dismissing for improper venue.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the ability to obtain § 101 dismissals even in cases with venue defects, creating precedent that may deter refiling of the same claims in a proper venue and providing collateral estoppel effects.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the risk that venue challenges will not merely result in transfer or refiling but will be coupled with substantive § 101 rulings that permanently dispose of their patent claims.
